questions.title: Computing Expected Credit Loss for a Counterparty
questions.prompt: A derivatives counterparty has a 2% probability of default over the next year, exposure at default of $10 million, and a loss given default of 60% (40% expected recovery). Compute the expected credit loss, and explain what each input would need to change for the expected loss to double.
questions.modelAnswer: Expected Loss = PD * LGD * EAD = 0.02 * 0.60 * $10,000,000 = $120,000. Because expected loss is a simple product of three independent inputs, doubling any one of them alone doubles the expected loss: PD rising to 4% (credit quality deteriorating), LGD rising to 120% is impossible since LGD is bounded at 100%, so a more realistic path to doubling via LGD alone would need a different, higher-LGD counterparty or collateral arrangement entirely, or EAD rising to $20 million (the exposure itself growing, for instance as uncleared derivatives move further in-the-money for the counterparty's benefit). In practice, expected loss can also double from a combination of smaller moves in more than one input simultaneously — for example, PD rising from 2% to 3% (a 50% increase) alongside EAD rising from $10 million to $13.3 million (a 33% increase) together produce roughly a doubling, which is a more realistic real-world scenario than any single input moving in isolation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd compute this as a straight multiplication and then immediately flag the bounded nature of LGD — it can't exceed 100%, so 'doubling LGD' only works as a lever within that ceiling, and for a counterparty already near a high LGD, the realistic way credit losses double is PD and EAD moving together, not any one input in isolation. That combination is also the more realistic failure mode I'd actually worry about: credit quality worsening (PD up) tends to happen alongside growing derivatives exposure (EAD up) in a real stress scenario, not independently.
questions.example: EL = 0.02 * 0.60 * 10,000,000 = $120,000. Doubling via PD alone: PD to 4%. Doubling via EAD alone: EAD to $20 million. LGD alone cannot double past 100%.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that LGD is capped at 100%, making 'doubling LGD alone' impossible in many cases
Treating the three inputs as always moving independently rather than considering realistic joint stress scenarios
Computing the multiplication incorrectly by mixing up LGD with the recovery rate (1-LGD)
Not recognizing expected loss as the simple product of the three inputs
keyPoints: Expected Loss = PD * LGD * EAD = $120,000 here
Doubling any one input alone doubles the expected loss, holding the others fixed
LGD is bounded at 100%, limiting how much it alone can rise
A realistic doubling scenario often involves PD and EAD rising together in a stress event

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the expected credit loss
Correctly identifies single-input paths to doubling, including the LGD cap
Proposes a realistic joint-input stress scenario

questions.title: Sharpe vs. Sortino for a Trend-Following Return Pattern
questions.prompt: A trend-following strategy has annualized mean return 9%, annualized total volatility 14%, and annualized downside deviation (below zero) of only 8%, with a 2% risk-free rate. Compute the Sharpe and Sortino ratios, and explain what the gap between them reveals about this strategy's return shape.
questions.code:
Sharpe = (mean - rf) / total_vol
Sortino = (mean - rf) / downside_dev
questions.modelAnswer: Sharpe = (0.09-0.02)/0.14 = 0.07/0.14 = 0.50. Sortino = (0.09-0.02)/0.08 = 0.07/0.08 = 0.875. The Sortino ratio is substantially higher than the Sharpe ratio, which reveals that a meaningful share of this strategy's total volatility comes from upside moves, not downside risk — exactly the asymmetric pattern a trend-following strategy is expected to produce: small, frequent losses during choppy, directionless markets, punctuated by rare, large gains when a real trend emerges and the strategy rides it. Sharpe penalizes that large upside volatility exactly as harshly as it would penalize an equally large downside move, understating how attractive this strategy's actual risk profile is; Sortino, by only counting downside deviation in the denominator, correctly recognizes that the upside volatility isn't something an investor would want penalized at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd compute both ratios and then immediately flag the gap as diagnostic rather than just reporting two numbers: a Sortino meaningfully above the Sharpe is the signature of positively-skewed, trend-following-style returns, where the 'risk' Sharpe penalizes is disproportionately upside volatility from rare big winners. I'd tell an allocator that Sharpe alone understates how attractive this specific return shape is, and that Sortino is the more honest number to quote for a strategy built exactly this way.
questions.example: Sharpe = 0.07/0.14 = 0.50. Sortino = 0.07/0.08 = 0.875 — a large gap signaling favorable (upside-heavy) return asymmetry.
commonMistakes: Computing one ratio correctly but making an arithmetic error on the other
Not connecting the Sharpe/Sortino gap specifically to trend-following's expected return shape
Assuming a Sortino higher than Sharpe is suspicious or an error rather than a meaningful, expected signal
Treating the two ratios as redundant rather than each answering a distinct question
keyPoints: Sharpe = 0.50; Sortino = 0.875
A Sortino well above Sharpe signals favorable, upside-heavy return asymmetry
This pattern matches trend-following's expected shape: frequent small losses, rare large gains
Sharpe penalizes upside volatility as much as downside, understating this strategy's true appeal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the Sharpe ratio
Correctly computes the Sortino ratio
Correctly interprets the gap in terms of return asymmetry
Connects the pattern to trend-following's expected behavior

questions.title: Computing and Interpreting the Calmar Ratio
questions.prompt: A strategy has an annualized return of 11% and a maximum drawdown of -22% over its backtest history. Compute its Calmar ratio, and explain one specific scenario where a strategy with a higher Calmar ratio than a competing strategy would still be the riskier one to allocate to.
questions.modelAnswer: Calmar = 0.11 / 0.22 = 0.50. The strategy earned about half its worst peak-to-trough decline, annualized. The scenario where a higher Calmar ratio can still mean a riskier allocation: Calmar is driven entirely by the single worst historical drawdown, and that number is especially unstable with a short backtest history — a strategy that happens to have a short track record which simply hasn't yet experienced its true worst-case scenario can show an artificially high Calmar ratio purely because the sample got lucky, not because the underlying strategy is actually safer. A second strategy with a longer track record and a lower Calmar ratio may have already lived through, and therefore already reflects, a genuinely representative worst case. Comparing Calmar ratios computed over very different sample lengths without adjusting for that is a direct way to be misled into thinking the short-history strategy is safer when it has simply not yet been tested by a bad enough scenario.
questions.professionalAnswer: Calmar is a useful number, but I'd never compare it across two strategies without first checking how long each backtest actually is — a short sample that hasn't lived through a real stress event will show an artificially flattering Calmar simply because its worst drawdown so far isn't its true worst-case drawdown yet. I'd want to see both strategies' max drawdown stress-tested against a common historical crisis period before trusting a Calmar comparison between them.
questions.example: Calmar = 0.11/0.22 = 0.50. A strategy with a 6-month backtest and Calmar of 0.9 isn't necessarily safer than one with a 10-year backtest and Calmar of 0.5 — the shorter sample simply hasn't been tested by a real crisis yet.
commonMistakes: Computing the Calmar ratio correctly but treating it as a complete, standalone risk measure
Not recognizing that Calmar is driven by a single historical event (the worst drawdown)
Comparing Calmar ratios across strategies with very different backtest lengths without adjustment
Assuming a higher Calmar ratio always implies lower real-world risk
keyPoints: Calmar = annualized return / abs(max drawdown) = 0.50 here
Calmar is driven entirely by one historical event: the single worst drawdown
A short backtest that hasn't experienced a real stress event can show an artificially high Calmar
Comparing Calmar ratios requires checking that both samples cover comparably severe historical periods

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the Calmar ratio
Correctly identifies the single-event instability of max drawdown
Describes a concrete, correct scenario where a higher Calmar misleads

questions.title: Diagnosing a Momentum Crash
questions.prompt: A 12-month momentum strategy that performed well for three years suddenly loses 25% in two weeks during a sharp market turning point, then partially recovers over the following months. Diagnose what happened and what, if anything, should change going forward.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the textbook momentum crash, a known and well-documented failure mode rather than a sign the strategy is broken. Momentum, by construction, is fully invested in whatever has recently performed well (long past winners) and against whatever has recently performed poorly (short past losers); at a sharp market turning point — particularly a rebound after a selloff — the prior losers can snap back violently while the prior winners stall or reverse, which is exactly the opposite of what the position is built to profit from, and it happens fast specifically because turning points are, by definition, abrupt and hard to react to in time. The two-week timeframe is consistent with this: momentum crashes tend to be sharp and concentrated rather than a slow grind, because they're driven by a rapid regime change the signal's 12-month lookback is far too slow to react to. The partial recovery afterward is also consistent with the pattern — once the turning point passes and a new trend establishes itself, the strategy's lookback eventually re-aligns with the new reality and resumes performing, assuming the strategy's edge is otherwise intact. Going forward, the realistic fix isn't to abandon momentum, but to size it with this known tail risk explicitly budgeted for — momentum crash risk is a structural feature of the strategy family, not an anomaly to be engineered away, and a volatility-scaling or drawdown-based de-risking overlay specifically for sharp reversals is the standard practical mitigation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd name this immediately as a momentum crash rather than treating it as an unexplained anomaly, because the pattern — sharp, fast loss at a market turning point, partial recovery after — is the specific, well-documented way this strategy family is known to fail. The lookback window that makes momentum work in trending markets is exactly what makes it slow to react when the trend violently reverses. I wouldn't recommend abandoning the strategy over one crash; I'd recommend sizing it with this tail risk explicitly budgeted for from the start, since a crash like this isn't a surprise to anyone who understood what family of strategy they were running.
commonMistakes: Treating the sharp loss as an unexplained anomaly rather than naming the known momentum crash pattern
Recommending abandoning momentum entirely rather than sizing for its known tail risk
Not connecting the two-week timeframe to the strategy's slow-reacting lookback window
Missing that the partial recovery afterward is itself consistent with the known pattern, not a separate surprise
keyPoints: Momentum crashes are a known, documented failure mode, not an anomaly
They occur at sharp market turning points, when prior losers snap back and prior winners stall or reverse
The strategy's lookback window is inherently too slow to react to an abrupt reversal in time
The practical mitigation is explicit sizing/budgeting for this known tail risk, not abandoning momentum

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the momentum crash mechanism

questions.title: Diagnosing a Correlated Carry Unwind
questions.prompt: A diversified portfolio of FX and futures carry trades, each individually small and stable, all lose money sharply on the same day, with correlations across the different carry positions spiking from near-zero historically to near-one that day. Diagnose what happened.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a classic carry crash, and the correlation spike is the key diagnostic signature. Carry trades across different currency pairs or futures curves are individually earning a yield for bearing a specific, narrow risk (an interest rate differential persisting, a curve staying in backwardation), and historically these risks are largely unrelated to each other, which is exactly why a diversified carry book shows low cross-position correlation most of the time. A risk-off shock changes that: a sudden flight to safety or spike in risk aversion causes positions that were held specifically because they 'got paid to wait' to be unwound broadly and simultaneously — not because each individual carry relationship broke, but because a common driver (risk appetite collapsing across the whole market) now dominates every position at once, which is exactly what correlation spiking from near-zero to near-one measures directly. This is a structural, well-documented feature of carry strategies, not a sign any individual trade was mispriced. Going forward, this means a 'diversified' carry book should not be treated as actually diversified during a risk-off shock — correlation estimates from calm periods systematically understate the true correlated tail risk, and risk budgeting or VaR models built on calm-period correlations will understate the book's true combined risk exactly when it matters most.
questions.professionalAnswer: The correlation spike is the whole story here — this is a carry crash, where positions that look unrelated in calm markets turn out to share a single hidden driver, risk appetite, that dominates everything the moment it flips. I wouldn't look for what went wrong with each individual carry trade, because nothing did; the diversification the book relied on was always conditional on calm markets, and a risk-off shock is precisely the condition under which that diversification disappears. The practical lesson is to stop trusting calm-period correlation estimates for tail-risk sizing on a carry book.
commonMistakes: Investigating each individual carry position for a specific error rather than recognizing the common driver
Missing that the correlation spike itself is the diagnostic signature of a carry crash
Treating this as a surprise rather than a well-documented structural feature of carry strategies
Not drawing the forward-looking implication that calm-period correlations understate true tail risk
keyPoints: Carry trades are individually earning compensation for narrow, historically unrelated risks
A risk-off shock introduces a common driver (collapsing risk appetite) that dominates every position at once
The correlation spike from near-zero to near-one is the direct signature of this common-driver unwind
Calm-period correlation estimates systematically understate true tail-risk correlation for carry books

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the carry crash mechanism
Correctly explains the correlation spike as the diagnostic signature
Frames this as a structural feature, not individual position errors

questions.title: A Combined Signal's IC Degrades Out of Sample
questions.prompt: A researcher combines three signals using IC-based weighting, and the combined signal's in-sample Information Coefficient is a strong 0.08. Out-of-sample, the combined IC drops to 0.01. Diagnose what likely happened and how to fix the combination process.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely explanation is that the IC-based weights themselves were estimated on the same data used to measure the strong in-sample result, making the weighting process itself a form of parameter fitting — exactly the overfitting risk the signal-combination lesson flags explicitly: a combination of signals that looks great because its weights were tuned on the full history is not meaningfully different from fitting any other parameter to a backtest. If the three underlying signals' individual ICs were themselves noisy or unstable, the IC-weighting step could have assigned disproportionate weight to whichever signal happened to look strongest in that specific in-sample window purely by chance, producing an in-sample combined IC that's optimistic in exactly the same way a best-of-many-parameters backtest is optimistic. A second, related possibility is that the three signals were more correlated with each other than the researcher checked for; if two of the three are highly correlated, the combination effectively double-counts one underlying driver, and if that driver happened to work well in-sample but not out-of-sample, the combination inherits that fragility. The fix: estimate combination weights only on a training period, strictly held out from the period used to measure the reported out-of-sample IC, and check pairwise signal correlations before combining — treating highly correlated signals as one, not two independent votes.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first question would be whether the IC weights were estimated on the same window being used to report the strong in-sample result — if so, that's the whole story, and it's the identical mistake as tuning any other backtest parameter on data you're also using to judge the result. I'd also check the correlation matrix between the three underlying signals before trusting the combination at all, since two highly correlated signals getting double-weighted toward whichever looked best in-sample is a very common, very quiet way this kind of degradation happens.
commonMistakes: Not checking whether the combination weights were estimated and evaluated on the same data window
Missing pairwise signal correlation as a contributing factor
Treating the IC degradation as evidence the whole approach of combining signals is flawed, rather than the specific estimation process
Not proposing a concrete fix involving a strict train/test split for the weighting step itself
keyPoints: IC-based combination weights estimated on the same data used to report results are themselves a fit parameter
This produces the same kind of optimistic bias as any in-sample-optimized backtest parameter
Highly correlated underlying signals can cause the combination to double-count one fragile driver
Fix: estimate weights only on a held-out training window, and check signal correlations before combining

questions.title: A High-Sharpe Backtest That Collapses Under Realistic Costs
questions.prompt: A daily-rebalanced strategy shows a backtested Sharpe ratio of 2.2 with zero transaction costs assumed. Once a realistic 10 bps round-trip cost is applied, the Sharpe drops to 0.3. Diagnose why this happened and what it implies about the strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a turnover problem, and the magnitude of the collapse is the tell. A strategy that rebalances daily pays its round-trip cost roughly 252 times a year; at 10 bps per round trip, that's a cost drag of roughly 25%+ annualized, which is large enough to erase most or all of a strategy whose raw, cost-free edge wasn't dramatically larger than that drag to begin with. The fact that the Sharpe collapsed from 2.2 to 0.3 rather than, say, 2.2 to 1.8, suggests the strategy's actual signal-driven edge was thin relative to its trading frequency — the backtest's headline Sharpe was mostly an artifact of ignoring the cost of acting on the signal as often as the signal fires, not a reflection of a genuinely strong, durable edge. This doesn't necessarily mean the underlying signal has zero information content; it means the specific implementation (rebalancing daily, trading the full position change every single day) is economically unviable at these cost levels. The fix path is either reducing turnover directly (trading less frequently, or adding a no-trade band so small signal changes don't trigger a full rebalance), or accepting that this specific signal, at this frequency, doesn't clear realistic costs and shouldn't be deployed as is.
questions.professionalAnswer: A drop this severe — 2.2 to 0.3 — tells me the headline Sharpe was almost entirely a turnover illusion, not a real edge that costs merely dented. Daily rebalancing at 10 bps round-trip is roughly a 25-point annual cost drag, and surviving that intact requires a genuinely large raw edge, which this strategy evidently didn't have. I'd look at reducing turnover specifically — a no-trade band, or rebalancing less frequently — before concluding the underlying signal is worthless, since the signal and the trading frequency are two separate design choices that got conflated here.

Not quantifying the actual annual cost drag implied by daily rebalancing at 10 bps round-trip
Treating the collapse as evidence of a backtest bug rather than an economically meaningful result
Not proposing turnover reduction (no-trade bands, less frequent rebalancing) as a concrete next step

A collapse this severe indicates the raw signal edge was thin relative to its trading frequency, not a backtest error
The headline cost-free Sharpe was largely a turnover-driven illusion
Reducing turnover (no-trade bands, less frequent rebalancing) is the concrete next step before abandoning the signal

questions.title: A Mean-Variance Optimizer Producing Extreme Concentrated Weights
questions.prompt: A mean-variance optimizer run on 40 stocks, given historical mean returns and a sample covariance matrix, outputs weights where three stocks each get over 40% of the portfolio and most others get near zero or negative weight. Diagnose why this happened and how you'd fix the construction process.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the well-known fragility of naive mean-variance optimization to estimation error in expected returns, not a sign anything is mathematically wrong with the optimizer. The optimizer is doing exactly what it's told: maximizing expected return for a given risk level using the inputs it's given, and it has no way of knowing that the input expected-return estimates themselves carry substantial sampling noise. Because the optimization is unconstrained, it will aggressively tilt toward whichever assets happen to have the highest estimated expected return and the most favorable estimated correlation structure — and small, essentially noise-driven differences in those estimates get amplified into large, extreme weight differences, which is precisely why three stocks dominating at 40%+ each while others get near-zero or negative weight is the textbook symptom of this problem rather than evidence of a genuinely superior risk-return tradeoff in those three names. The fix is standard: either constrain position weights (capping any single position at some reasonable maximum), use a shrinkage estimator that pulls the noisy expected-return estimates toward a more stable prior (such as the cross-sectional average), or fall back to a simpler, less input-sensitive construction method like inverse-volatility or risk-parity weighting, which several of the earlier lessons in this course note frequently outperforms 'optimal' mean-variance weights out-of-sample precisely because it depends on far fewer noisy inputs.
questions.professionalAnswer: This result is the mean-variance optimizer's well-known Achilles' heel, not a bug: it's extremely sensitive to small estimation errors in expected returns, and extreme, concentrated weights like this are the textbook symptom of that sensitivity, not evidence those three stocks are genuinely special. I'd fix this with position caps and a shrinkage estimator on the expected-return inputs before trusting the optimizer's output again, and I'd seriously consider whether a simpler method like inverse-volatility weighting would actually perform better out-of-sample here, since it depends on far fewer noisy inputs.
commonMistakes: Assuming the optimizer found a genuinely superior allocation rather than diagnosing estimation-error sensitivity
Not naming position constraints or shrinkage as the standard fixes
Blaming the covariance matrix when the more common driver of extreme weights is noisy expected-return estimates
Not considering a simpler, less input-sensitive construction method as an alternative
keyPoints: Mean-variance optimization is highly sensitive to estimation error in expected returns
Extreme, concentrated weights are a textbook symptom of that sensitivity, not a genuinely superior allocation
Standard fixes: position weight caps and shrinkage estimators on expected returns
Simpler methods like inverse-volatility weighting are often more robust out-of-sample

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses estimation-error sensitivity as the root cause
Correctly explains why small input errors produce extreme output weights
Proposes position constraints and/or shrinkage as concrete fixes
Considers a simpler alternative construction method

questions.title: A Drawdown That Hasn't Recovered by the End of the Sample
questions.prompt: A strategy's backtest ends with the equity curve still 9% below its prior peak, with no clear sign of recovery in the final months of the sample. How should a risk manager interpret this, and what should they do before approving the strategy for live capital?
questions.modelAnswer: An unresolved drawdown at the end of a backtest sample is a genuinely important, uncomfortable fact that shouldn't be smoothed over by reporting the max drawdown percentage alone — a strategy can show a respectable max drawdown number while still being, as of the most recent data, unresolved as to whether that drawdown is temporary or the start of a more permanent edge decay. The risk manager's first job is to not assume it's temporary: an unresolved drawdown with no sign of recovery is exactly as consistent with 'this edge has genuinely stopped working' (strategy decay) as it is with 'this is a normal, if currently uncomfortable, drawdown that will resolve given more time.' The data in hand, by construction, cannot tell these two explanations apart — that requires either a longer post-drawdown sample, or an independent diagnosis of whether anything about the strategy's underlying market assumption has structurally changed. Before approving live capital, the risk manager should extend the testing or paper-trading period specifically to observe whether the drawdown resolves, investigate whether the strategy's core assumption has changed in a way that would explain persistent underperformance, and in any case should size the initial live allocation conservatively, explicitly treating the current unresolved drawdown as the realistic starting state rather than assuming the strategy will immediately resume its earlier, healthier performance.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't approve this for live capital as is — an unresolved drawdown sitting at the very end of the backtest sample is exactly the kind of fact that gets quietly dropped when someone reports 'max drawdown was only 9%' without mentioning it never actually recovered. The honest position is that the data can't yet tell you whether this is a normal drawdown or the start of real decay, and I'd want either more time (extended paper trading) or a specific investigation into whether the strategy's core assumption still holds, before sizing any live allocation — and even then, I'd size conservatively given that the most recent evidence is still underwater.
commonMistakes: Reporting only the max drawdown percentage without flagging that it's unresolved at the end of the sample
Assuming the drawdown is temporary without evidence either way
Approving live capital without extending the observation period or investigating a possible structural change
Sizing the initial live allocation as if the strategy's healthier historical average performance, not the current unresolved state, is the realistic starting point
keyPoints: An unresolved drawdown at the end of a sample cannot, by itself, distinguish a temporary dip from genuine edge decay
Reporting only the max drawdown percentage without this context is misleading
Extending the observation period or investigating structural changes is needed before approving live capital
Any initial live sizing should conservatively reflect the current unresolved state, not the historical average

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the ambiguity between temporary drawdown and genuine decay
Flags the risk of reporting max drawdown without this context
Proposes extending observation or investigating structural change before approval
Recommends conservative initial sizing given the unresolved state

questions.title: A Fake 'Crash' From Unadjusted Split Data
questions.prompt: A backtest shows a stock apparently losing 50% of its value overnight with no corresponding news, and the strategy incorrectly triggers a large short position. Diagnose the likely data issue and the correct fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A sudden, overnight 50% price drop with no corresponding news is the classic signature of an unadjusted stock split in the raw price data — a 2-for-1 split, for instance, halves the per-share price overnight while leaving the company's total market value and the shareholder's total position value completely unchanged, but a raw, unadjusted price series shows this purely mechanical event as if the stock had crashed. The strategy's short-triggering logic reacted to what looks like a genuine, dramatic price decline, when nothing about the underlying business actually changed at all. The fix is to use adjusted close prices rather than raw close prices for any return-based calculation: historical prices should be rescaled backward through time specifically so that splits, dividends, and other corporate actions don't create artificial jumps or gaps in the series the strategy's signal or risk logic is watching. Before trusting the backtest's results at all, every other apparent large move in the historical dataset should be cross-checked against actual corporate-action records, not just this one, since an unadjusted split is one of the most common and easiest-to-miss sources of a corrupted backtest signal.
questions.professionalAnswer: A 50% overnight move with zero news is almost always a data problem, not a market event, and a stock split is the first thing I'd check — it produces exactly this signature, a price cut in half with the company's actual value completely unchanged. The fix is mechanical: switch to adjusted close prices for any return calculation, and then audit the rest of the dataset for the same issue, because if one split slipped through unadjusted, there's a good chance others did too.
commonMistakes: Investigating the trading strategy's logic before checking for a basic data quality issue
Not recognizing the specific signature of an unadjusted split (overnight price halving with no news)
Fixing only the one flagged incident rather than auditing the dataset for other unadjusted corporate actions
Confusing a stock split with a dividend or other corporate action that would produce a different-shaped artifact
keyPoints: An overnight large price move with no news is a classic signature of an unadjusted corporate action, often a stock split
A split changes share count and per-share price mechanically, with no change in total value
The fix is using adjusted close prices for all return-based calculations
The rest of the dataset should be audited for the same issue, not just the one flagged incident

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies an unadjusted corporate action as the likely cause
Correctly explains why a split produces this specific signature
Proposes the correct fix (adjusted close prices)
Recommends auditing the broader dataset for the same issue

questions.title: Designing a Signal Pipeline That Structurally Prevents Lookahead
questions.prompt: Design a signal-construction pipeline for a research team of five analysts, where the single most common bug historically has been accidental lookahead from a misplaced shift. What would you build so the bug becomes structurally hard to introduce, not just documented against?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd standardize the three-stage pipeline — transform, normalize, lag — as a shared library function every analyst calls rather than a pattern each analyst re-implements by hand, because the lag step is exactly the one line most prone to being forgotten or misplaced, and centralizing it removes the chance of each analyst getting it subtly wrong in their own code. Concretely, I'd build a `finalize_signal()` function that takes a raw, normalized signal and automatically applies the forward shift internally, so that no analyst-facing code path ever touches a signal that hasn't already been lagged — the lag becomes the library's responsibility, not each analyst's memory. On top of that, I'd add an automated check that runs on every submitted signal before it's allowed into a backtest: verify that the signal's timestamp index, after lagging, never aligns with or precedes the return it's meant to predict, flagging a hard error (not just a warning) if it does. Finally, I'd require every new signal to pass a known-answer test — a synthetic dataset with an injected, deliberately placed future shock that a correctly-lagged signal should not react to on the day it occurs — as a release gate before the signal is trusted in any shared backtest.
questions.professionalAnswer: The principle I'd apply is: don't rely on five people remembering to do the same tricky thing correctly every time — make the correct behavior the only behavior the shared code path allows. That means a shared `finalize_signal()` function that bakes the lag in internally, an automated timestamp-alignment check that hard-fails before a signal reaches any backtest, and a known-answer synthetic test with an injected future shock that every new signal has to pass before anyone trusts it. If the lag depends on each analyst remembering to write `.shift(1)` correctly in their own notebook, it will eventually be forgotten, and the fix has to be structural, not a reminder in a wiki page.
commonMistakes: Relying on documentation or a checklist rather than a structural, code-enforced fix
Not centralizing the lag step into a shared function that every analyst must use
Missing an automated, pre-backtest check that would catch the bug even if introduced
Not including a concrete test case (e.g., a known-answer synthetic test) as a release gate
keyPoints: Centralize the lag step into a shared, mandatory pipeline function rather than per-analyst code
Add an automated timestamp-alignment check that hard-fails before a signal reaches any backtest
Require a known-answer synthetic test with an injected future shock as a release gate
The design goal is making the correct behavior the only behavior, not just documenting the correct behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes centralizing the lag step into shared, mandatory code
Proposes an automated pre-backtest alignment check
Proposes a concrete test case as a release gate
Articulates the structural-over-procedural design principle

questions.title: Designing a Fill-Simulation Layer for an Event-Driven Backtester
questions.prompt: Design the fill-simulation layer of an event-driven backtester that needs to correctly handle market orders, limit orders, and stop orders, each with their own realistic fill logic. What would the architecture look like?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd design this as a dedicated fill-simulation module, separate from the signal and portfolio-construction logic, that takes a submitted order (with its type, price if applicable, and size) and the next bar's OHLC data, and returns a fill decision and fill price according to order-type-specific rules — never a single, one-size-fits-all 'fills at the signal price' shortcut. For a market order, the fill price is next-bar open, with slippage and impact models layered on top as a separate, explicit adjustment. For a limit order, the module checks whether the bar's actual traded range (low for a buy limit, high for a sell limit) crossed the limit price; if not, the order carries forward unfilled rather than being marked filled just because the signal fired. For a stop order, the module checks whether price moved through the stop level, and if triggered, converts the order into a market order for that same bar's remaining fill logic, inheriting the market order's slippage model rather than filling exactly at the stop price. Each order type's logic lives in its own clearly separated function with its own unit tests, specifically so that a strategy built around limit orders can never be accidentally backtested using market-order fill assumptions, and vice versa — that mismatch is exactly the kind of bug that produces an unrealistic backtest without anyone noticing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep this strictly separate from everything else in the backtester and give each order type its own explicit, testable fill function rather than one generic 'did it fill' check. Market orders fill at next-bar open plus slippage; limit orders only fill if the bar's actual range crossed the limit; stops convert to market orders once triggered and inherit market-order slippage. The architectural risk I'd guard against hardest is a strategy conceived around one order type accidentally getting backtested with another type's fill logic — that mismatch tests a strategy that doesn't actually exist, and it's an easy mistake to make if the fill logic isn't cleanly separated by order type from the start.
commonMistakes: Using one generic fill rule for all order types instead of distinct, order-type-specific logic
Not checking a limit order's fill against the bar's actual traded range
Not having a stop order inherit market-order slippage once triggered
Mixing fill-simulation logic into the signal or portfolio-construction code rather than keeping it a separate module
keyPoints: Fill simulation should be a separate module taking order type, price, size, and next-bar OHLC as input
Market orders fill at next-bar open plus slippage, not at the signal price
Limit orders only fill if the bar's actual range crossed the limit price
Stop orders convert to market orders once triggered, inheriting market-order slippage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a correctly separated, order-type-specific fill module
Correctly specifies market order fill logic
Correctly specifies limit order fill logic using the bar's traded range
Correctly specifies stop order conversion and slippage inheritance

questions.title: Designing a Combined Futures-and-Options Hedging Program
questions.prompt: A commodity producer wants to hedge both the linear price risk of their expected production and the risk of a sudden, severe price drop, while acknowledging the hedge instruments don't perfectly match their physical product. Design the hedging program.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd split this into two distinct, complementary layers rather than trying to solve both risks with one instrument. The linear price risk — the bulk of the exposure, where a futures or forward contract moves roughly one-for-one against the expected production — gets a static or periodically-rebalanced short futures position sized to the expected production volume; this is the base layer and addresses most of the exposure cheaply. On top of that, for protection against a severe, sudden price drop specifically (a tail scenario the linear futures hedge already covers in expectation but where the producer may want an explicit floor), I'd add a long put option position, since puts specifically cap downside without requiring the producer to give up upside the way a pure short-futures position inherently does on the full notional. Because the available futures and options may be written on a related but not identical underlying (basis risk, if there's no liquid contract on the producer's exact product grade or delivery location), I'd explicitly quantify and report the expected basis risk — the correlation and historical tracking error between the hedge instrument and the actual physical product — rather than presenting the hedge as a complete solution; a cross-hedge reduces risk substantially but doesn't eliminate it, and the program should be sized and communicated with that explicitly acknowledged, not glossed over.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this in two layers: a futures-based linear hedge sized to expected production as the base layer, and a long put overlay specifically for tail protection against a severe price drop, since puts cap the downside without forcing the producer to give up all upside the way a pure futures hedge does. The part I wouldn't skip is being explicit about basis risk — if the available contracts aren't a perfect match for the producer's exact product, I'd quantify that mismatch and report it as a real, remaining risk, not something the hedging program makes disappear.
commonMistakes: Trying to solve both the linear exposure and the tail-risk protection with a single instrument
Not explaining why options (puts), not just more futures, are the right tool for the specific tail-protection need
Presenting the hedge as eliminating risk entirely rather than explicitly quantifying remaining basis risk
Not sizing the futures layer specifically to the expected production volume
keyPoints: Linear exposure is hedged with a futures/forward position sized to expected production
Severe-downside protection is better served by a long put overlay, which caps losses without full upside sacrifice
The two layers are complementary, not substitutes for each other
Basis risk from imperfect hedge-instrument matching must be explicitly quantified and reported, not hidden

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the linear futures-based hedge layer
Correctly designs the put-option-based tail-protection layer
Explains why the two layers are complementary
Explicitly addresses and quantifies basis risk

questions.title: Designing Adjusted-Price Handling in a Backtesting Data Pipeline
questions.prompt: Design how a backtesting data pipeline should ingest, store, and serve historical equity prices so that stock splits, dividends, and other corporate actions never silently corrupt a strategy's return calculations.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd store both raw and adjusted prices side by side rather than only the adjusted series, since some use cases (reconciling against actual historical trade confirmations, for instance) genuinely need the raw, as-traded price, while almost every return calculation and backtest should default to the adjusted series. The adjustment itself should be computed and stored as its own versioned pipeline step — a corporate-actions table recording every split, dividend, and other adjustment event with its effective date — rather than hard-coded into whichever script happens to load the price data, so that a correction to one adjustment factor propagates consistently everywhere the adjusted series is used, instead of requiring every downstream script to be patched individually. The data-serving layer (whatever function or API hands prices to a backtest) should default to serving adjusted prices and require an explicit, deliberate flag to request raw prices, making the safe choice the path of least resistance rather than something an analyst has to remember to ask for. Finally, I'd add an automated check that flags any single-day return exceeding a configurable threshold (e.g., 25%) with no corresponding, recorded corporate action or extreme market event, since an unexplained large move is almost always a sign the adjustment pipeline missed something.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep raw and adjusted prices both in the data store, compute adjustments from a single versioned corporate-actions table rather than ad hoc per-script logic, and make adjusted prices the default that every backtest gets unless someone explicitly asks for raw. The safeguard I'd add on top is an automated large-single-day-move flag with no matching recorded corporate action — that's the cheapest, most reliable way to catch a missed split or dividend adjustment before it corrupts a strategy's signal, rather than discovering it only after a strategy makes a bad trade off bad data.
commonMistakes: Storing only adjusted prices with no way to reconcile against raw, as-traded data
Hard-coding adjustment logic into individual scripts rather than a single, versioned corporate-actions source
Making raw prices the default and adjusted prices something an analyst has to explicitly request
Not including an automated check to catch unexplained large single-day moves
keyPoints: Store both raw and adjusted prices, with adjusted as the default for backtesting
Compute adjustments from a single, versioned corporate-actions table, not per-script logic
Make the safe (adjusted) choice the path of least resistance in the serving layer
Add an automated check flagging unexplained large single-day moves with no recorded corporate action

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs storage of both raw and adjusted prices
Correctly centralizes adjustment logic into a single versioned source
Makes adjusted prices the safe default in the serving layer
Proposes an automated anomaly check for unexplained large moves

questions.title: Designing a Three-Lines-of-Defense Structure for a Growing Trading Firm
questions.prompt: A trading firm has grown from 10 to 80 people and still has no formal risk governance structure beyond the founder's personal oversight. Design a three-lines-of-defense structure appropriate for this stage, and explain what each line is specifically responsible for.
questions.modelAnswer: The first line is the trading desks themselves: they take the risk, and they own it day to day — each desk should have explicit, documented position and loss limits that they operate within, not informal verbal understandings with the founder. The second line is a genuinely independent risk and compliance function, reporting separately from the trading desks (not embedded within them, and not reporting through the same management chain as the desks it's meant to monitor), responsible for setting those limits in the first place, monitoring real-time adherence, and escalating breaches — at this size, this likely means hiring a dedicated risk officer rather than continuing to rely on the founder's personal, informal oversight, since that doesn't scale and creates a single point of failure. The third line is internal audit, which periodically and independently verifies that the first two lines are actually functioning as designed — at 80 people, this might start as a part-time or outsourced function rather than a large internal team, but it needs genuine independence from both the desks and the risk function it's checking, otherwise it can't catch a failure in the second line itself. The critical design principle across all three: each line needs real organizational independence from the one below it, not just a different job title under the same reporting chain, because the entire point of the structure is that no single failure point (including a well-intentioned but overworked founder) is the only thing standing between the firm and an unmanaged risk.
questions.professionalAnswer: At this size, informal founder oversight has almost certainly become the single point of failure, so I'd formalize all three lines with real organizational independence, not just new job titles. First line: desks operate within documented, specific limits, not verbal understandings. Second line: a dedicated risk officer, reporting separately from the desks, who actually sets and monitors those limits. Third line: an independent audit function, even if initially part-time or outsourced, specifically checking that the first two lines are doing their jobs — because the whole point of this structure is removing any single person, including the founder, as the only backstop.
commonMistakes: Proposing a risk function that still reports through the same chain as the trading desks it monitors
Not recognizing informal founder oversight as a single point of failure that needs to be formalized
Skipping the third line (audit) entirely rather than scaling it appropriately for an 80-person firm
Describing the three lines generically without specifying what each one is concretely responsible for
keyPoints: First line: trading desks operate within documented, specific limits, not informal understandings
Second line: an independent risk/compliance function, organizationally separate from the desks, that sets and monitors limits
Third line: an independent audit function (can start small/part-time) verifying the first two lines actually work
Each line needs genuine organizational independence, not just a different job title under the same chain

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly specifies the first line's responsibilities
Correctly specifies the second line's responsibilities and independence requirement
Correctly specifies the third line's responsibilities and independence requirement
Identifies informal founder oversight as the single point of failure being addressed

questions.title: Designing a VWAP-Based Execution Architecture for a Capacity-Constrained Strategy
questions.prompt: A strategy's research has identified a signal with genuine edge, but the position sizes needed are large relative to daily volume in several names. Design the execution architecture that lets this strategy trade without destroying its own edge through market impact.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd architect this as a separate execution layer sitting between the signal/portfolio-construction layer and the market, rather than letting the signal logic submit full-size orders directly. The execution layer takes a target position change from the portfolio construction step and breaks it into smaller child orders sized in proportion to each name's typical historical volume profile throughout the trading day — a VWAP-style approach — rather than submitting the full order at once or splitting it evenly over time regardless of liquidity (which a TWAP approach would do, trading too heavily during naturally thin periods). For the names where the required size is largest relative to ADV, the execution layer should also enforce an explicit participation-rate cap — never representing more than some fixed percentage of expected volume in any given interval — even if that means the position takes multiple days to fully build, since the whole point of this architecture is trading impact cost off against execution speed rather than always rushing to full size immediately. I'd also feed real-time fill data back into a monitoring component that tracks realized slippage against the pre-trade cost estimate, so that if actual impact is running meaningfully worse than the model predicted for a given name, the execution layer can automatically throttle back the participation rate rather than mechanically continuing a schedule that's proving more expensive than planned.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put a dedicated execution layer between the signal and the market that breaks large target positions into VWAP-style child orders sized to each name's typical intraday volume curve, with an explicit participation-rate cap for the names where the position is largest relative to ADV — accepting that some positions simply take multiple days to build rather than forcing full size immediately. The feedback loop I'd insist on is real-time slippage monitoring against the pre-trade cost model, so the system throttles itself back automatically on a name where actual impact is running worse than expected, instead of blindly following a fixed schedule into a cost blowout.
commonMistakes: Letting the signal/portfolio-construction layer submit full-size orders directly rather than through a dedicated execution layer
Using a flat TWAP schedule rather than a volume-proportional VWAP approach for names where liquidity varies across the day
Not enforcing an explicit participation-rate cap for the largest, most capacity-constrained positions
Missing a real-time feedback loop that throttles execution when realized slippage exceeds the pre-trade estimate
keyPoints: A dedicated execution layer breaks large target positions into volume-proportional (VWAP-style) child orders
An explicit participation-rate cap governs the most capacity-constrained names, even if it extends execution over multiple days
Impact cost is deliberately traded off against execution speed, not always rushed to full size
Real-time slippage monitoring against the pre-trade cost model should automatically throttle execution when impact runs worse than expected

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs a separate execution layer with VWAP-style child orders
Correctly specifies a participation-rate cap for capacity-constrained names
Explains the impact-vs-speed tradeoff explicitly
Proposes a real-time slippage feedback/throttling mechanism

questions.title: Designing a Market-Making Quoting Engine That Widens With Risk
questions.prompt: Design a simple market-making quoting engine's logic for setting the bid-ask spread dynamically, incorporating inventory risk and the possibility of trading against better-informed counterparties.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd design the quote as a base spread (covering order-processing cost, which is roughly constant) plus two dynamic adjustment terms layered on top. The first term scales with the market maker's current inventory position: as the firm accumulates a larger net long or short position relative to its target, the quoting engine should skew the quote — tightening the side that reduces inventory (to encourage trades back toward neutral) and widening the side that would increase inventory further (to discourage adding to an already-large position) — directly implementing the inventory-risk component of the spread. The second term scales with a real-time estimate of adverse selection risk, proxied by recent realized volatility or the recent frequency and size of one-sided order flow; when volatility or persistent one-directional flow spikes, the probability of trading against better-informed counterparties rises, and the engine should widen the overall spread symmetrically to compensate, independent of the inventory skew. I'd keep these as two separate, independently tunable adjustment terms rather than one blended parameter, specifically because inventory risk calls for an asymmetric, directional skew in the quote while adverse-selection risk calls for a symmetric widening — conflating the two into one number would make the engine unable to express 'I want to reduce my long position' and 'the market just got more dangerous to trade in' as the two separate signals they actually are.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as a base spread plus two independently-tunable adjustments: an inventory-skew term that tightens the side reducing the position and widens the side growing it, and a separate adverse-selection widening term driven by real-time volatility or one-sided flow that symmetrically widens both sides. Keeping these as two separate terms matters architecturally — inventory risk wants an asymmetric skew, adverse selection wants a symmetric widening, and collapsing them into one knob would make the engine unable to express both signals independently when they diverge, which they often do.
commonMistakes: Using a single, static spread that doesn't respond to inventory or market conditions at all
Conflating inventory-driven skew and adverse-selection-driven widening into one blended adjustment
Applying the inventory adjustment symmetrically rather than as a directional skew toward reducing the position
Not proposing a concrete, real-time proxy for adverse selection risk (e.g., volatility or one-sided flow)
keyPoints: Base spread covers order-processing cost; two dynamic terms adjust on top of it
Inventory risk produces an asymmetric skew: tighten the side reducing the position, widen the side growing it
Adverse selection risk produces a symmetric widening, driven by a real-time proxy like volatility or one-sided flow
The two adjustments should be independently tunable, not collapsed into one parameter

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the base spread plus adjustment structure
Correctly designs the inventory-driven directional skew
Correctly designs the adverse-selection-driven symmetric widening
Explains why the two adjustments should remain independently tunable

questions.title: Explaining a Modest Information Coefficient to a Skeptical PM
questions.prompt: A portfolio manager looks at your new signal's measured Information Coefficient of 0.04 and says, 'That's basically nothing.' How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd agree that 0.04 sounds small in isolation and explain why that's actually the normal, expected scale for a genuinely useful cross-sectional equity signal — ICs in the 0.02-0.08 range are common for signals that are real and add value, because this is fundamentally a game of small, repeatable edges applied across a large universe and many periods, not a game of big, individually obvious predictions. I'd walk through what actually matters beyond the raw number: is the IC stable in sign and magnitude across time (an IC that flips sign from period to period is a red flag regardless of its average size), and how does this signal's correlation with signals already in the book look (a modestly-sized but genuinely uncorrelated signal can meaningfully improve the combined portfolio's risk-adjusted return even at this scale). I'd also be direct that a single number, taken alone, isn't the whole story — I'd want to show the IC's consistency over time and its correlation profile against the existing signal set before asking the PM to make a capital-allocation decision based on the headline number alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't argue that 0.04 is secretly a big number — I'd explain why it's the right scale to expect here: this is a large cross-sectional universe, repeated every period, and ICs in the 0.02-0.08 range are exactly where real, useful signals tend to live. What I'd actually show the PM, rather than just defending the headline number, is the IC's stability over time and how uncorrelated it is with what's already in the book — because a small, stable, uncorrelated signal is a genuinely different and more valuable thing than a small, unstable, redundant one, and the raw IC number alone doesn't tell you which this is.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive and simply insisting the number is actually good without explaining why
Not providing the correct context for what a typical, useful cross-sectional IC actually looks like
Failing to raise IC stability over time and correlation with existing signals as the more important follow-up questions
Treating the single headline IC number as sufficient to settle the conversation on its own
keyPoints: ICs in the 0.02-0.08 range are typical for genuinely useful cross-sectional equity signals, not an anomaly
IC stability over time matters as much as its average magnitude
Correlation with existing signals in the book determines the signal's real incremental value
A single IC number alone shouldn't drive a capital allocation decision without this additional context

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly contextualizes typical IC magnitude for cross-sectional signals
Raises IC stability over time as a key additional consideration
Raises correlation with existing signals as a key additional consideration
Avoids defensiveness while still making a substantive case

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Analyst on Comparing Offers Across Firm Types
questions.prompt: A junior analyst you're mentoring has offers from a bank and a prop trading firm with similar headline total compensation, and asks you which is 'better.' How do you guide the conversation?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by pointing out that 'similar headline total compensation' can hide very different structures: a bank's pay is typically base-plus-bonus, with the bonus influenced by overall bank and division performance and relatively more predictable year to year; a prop trading firm's pay often ties more directly to the P&L the individual or desk generates, which can mean significantly higher upside in a strong year but also significantly more downside variance in a weak one. I'd ask the analyst directly how much variance in year-to-year pay they're comfortable with, since that's the real tradeoff being disguised by two similar-looking headline numbers. Beyond compensation structure, I'd push the conversation toward the things that actually determine whether the next few years go well: what the day-to-day role actually looks like at each firm (not just the title), whether there's real mentorship and a deliberate learning path, and what the firm's calibration around risk and honesty about results feels like — all things the headline comp number says nothing about, and all things I'd encourage the analyst to actually ask current employees at each firm about directly, rather than guessing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd steer the analyst away from 'which number is bigger' and toward 'which compensation structure matches how much variance you're comfortable with' — a bank's base-plus-bonus is more stable, a prop shop's P&L-linked pay has more upside and more downside, and those are genuinely different things even if this year's headline numbers happen to match. Then I'd push past compensation entirely: ask about actual day-to-day responsibilities, real mentorship, and how the firm handles being wrong about something, because those are the things that determine whether this is a good decision in a way the comp number alone can't tell you.
commonMistakes: Treating similar headline compensation numbers as making the two offers equivalent
Not explaining the structural difference in how bank versus prop firm compensation is typically driven
Skipping the analyst's own risk tolerance for pay variance as a relevant factor
Not pushing the conversation toward non-compensation factors like mentorship and day-to-day role content
keyPoints: Similar headline compensation can hide very different underlying structures and variance
Bank pay tends to be more stable; prop-firm pay tends to be more directly tied to individual/desk P&L
The analyst's own comfort with year-to-year pay variance is a legitimate, relevant factor
Non-compensation factors (actual role content, mentorship, risk culture) matter as much as the number

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Discretionary Override of a Systematic Signal
questions.prompt: A junior colleague wants to manually override a systematic strategy's position today because 'it just feels wrong given the news.' How do you handle this conversation?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd take the instinct seriously rather than dismissing it outright, because a genuine, well-reasoned concern about today's news is worth hearing out — but I'd separate that from the actual decision of whether to override a systematic position, which is a different and much higher-stakes question. The core issue with ad hoc discretionary overrides of a systematic strategy is that the entire value of running systematically is removing exactly this kind of in-the-moment, emotionally-influenced judgment call, which is precisely when human intuition is least reliable and hardest to later evaluate honestly — if the override works out, it reinforces overriding again next time for the wrong reasons; if it doesn't, it's hard to disentangle from ordinary bad luck. I'd ask: is this a genuinely new piece of information the systematic signal's inputs don't and structurally can't see (in which case the right fix is improving the signal or adding a formal risk override rule, not an ad hoc one-off decision), or is this an emotional reaction to news that the strategy's historical backtest already implicitly lived through similar versions of many times. If it's the latter, I'd push back directly and keep the systematic position as designed; if it's genuinely the former, I'd escalate it as a process or signal-design discussion, not a quiet, undocumented override made under time pressure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd hear out the specific concern, but I'd draw a hard line between 'this feels wrong' and 'this is a documented reason the systematic signal structurally can't account for.' Ad hoc overrides made under time pressure and emotional reaction are exactly the failure mode systematic trading exists to prevent, and if we start overriding whenever something 'feels wrong,' we've quietly turned a systematic strategy into a discretionary one without admitting it. If there's a real, new information gap, that's a conversation about improving the process or adding a formal rule — not a one-off call made today under pressure.

Allowing an ad hoc override without distinguishing genuinely new information from an emotional reaction
Not explaining why overrides made under time pressure are specifically unreliable and hard to evaluate afterward

Ad hoc overrides are hard to evaluate honestly afterward, whether they work out or not
The key diagnostic question: is this genuinely new information the signal can't see, or an emotional reaction
A real information gap should become a formal process or signal-design change, not a quiet one-off override

questions.title: Explaining Basis Risk to an Unhappy Hedging Client
questions.prompt: A client who hedged jet fuel exposure with crude oil futures is upset that their hedge didn't perfectly offset a recent loss, and asks why they paid for a hedge that 'didn't work.' How do you explain this?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by acknowledging the gap is real and explaining exactly why it exists rather than suggesting the hedge was somehow defective: there is no sufficiently liquid jet-fuel futures market, so the hedge was built using crude oil futures as a related but not identical instrument — this is a deliberate, disclosed design choice called cross-hedging, not an error, and it comes with basis risk, the risk that the hedging instrument doesn't move exactly in lockstep with the actual exposure. I'd show concretely what the hedge did accomplish: it substantially reduced the client's exposure to the dominant, shared driver of both crude and jet fuel prices (broad energy market moves), even though it couldn't capture the portion of jet fuel's price move that came from factors specific to jet fuel alone (refining margins, regional jet fuel supply-demand, seasonal travel demand) that crude oil futures have no exposure to at all. I'd reframe the conversation around what the hedge was always designed to do — reduce, not eliminate, risk — and if the client wants tighter protection, I'd discuss whether a different, more targeted (and likely more expensive or less liquid) instrument exists, or whether the existing cross-hedge ratio needs recalibrating based on the latest relationship between the two prices.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be upfront that this gap is expected, not a sign the hedge failed — there's no liquid jet-fuel futures market, so crude oil futures were always a cross-hedge, and cross-hedges reduce risk substantially without eliminating it, which is a real, known tradeoff we made deliberately, not an unexpected flaw. I'd show the client specifically how much of their exposure to the shared, broad energy-market driver the hedge did capture, and be honest that the portion of the move specific to jet fuel alone was never something crude oil futures could hedge — then talk about whether a tighter, more targeted instrument is worth the cost for next time.
commonMistakes: Implying the hedge was defective or failed rather than explaining basis risk as an expected, disclosed tradeoff
Not naming cross-hedging and basis risk specifically as the mechanism at play
Failing to show concretely what portion of the exposure the hedge did successfully reduce
Not offering a constructive forward-looking option (a more targeted instrument or a recalibrated hedge ratio)

A constructive next step (a more targeted instrument or recalibrated ratio) should be offered, not just an explanation

questions.title: Telling a Trader the Desk's Quotes Need to Widen
questions.prompt: A market-making trader resists your recommendation to widen quoted spreads during a period of rising volatility, worried about losing volume to competitors. How do you make the case?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd acknowledge the real concern directly — losing volume to a competitor who doesn't widen is a legitimate worry, not something to dismiss — but I'd walk through why staying tight in rising volatility is specifically dangerous, not just generically cautious: the bid-ask spread exists to compensate for inventory risk and adverse selection, and both rise mechanically as volatility rises. A quote that was appropriately priced in calm conditions becomes underpriced risk the moment volatility jumps, because the same spread is now compensating for a bigger expected cost of holding inventory and a higher probability of trading against someone who has better information about where the price is actually headed. I'd frame the tradeoff honestly: yes, some volume may go to a competitor willing to underprice their own risk during the volatile period, but the alternative is capturing that volume at a spread that doesn't actually compensate for the risk being taken on — which isn't really 'winning' the volume, it's subsidizing it. I'd rather lose some volume temporarily than win volume at a systematically unprofitable price.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd validate the competitive concern and then make the risk case plainly: the spread's whole job is compensating for inventory risk and adverse selection, and both of those go up mechanically when volatility rises, so a spread that was fine yesterday is underpriced risk today. If a competitor is willing to keep quoting tight anyway, that's their risk to carry, not evidence we should match them — winning volume at a price that doesn't cover the risk we're taking isn't actually winning anything.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the trader's competitive concern rather than acknowledging it as legitimate
Not explaining specifically why inventory risk and adverse selection both rise with volatility
Framing this as generic caution rather than a concrete repricing of a specific, rising cost
Not directly addressing the tradeoff between losing volume and taking on underpriced risk

Losing some volume to a competitor who underprices their own risk is a reasonable tradeoff, not a loss

questions.title: Convincing a Resistant Junior Researcher to Write a Hypothesis First
questions.prompt: A junior researcher wants to skip writing a formal hypothesis and just 'try a few versions and see what works,' arguing it would save time. How do you convince them otherwise?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd acknowledge that writing a formal hypothesis does take real time upfront, and I wouldn't pretend otherwise — the case for it isn't that it's free, it's that skipping it is far more expensive later, just in a way that's easy to miss in the moment. 'Try a few versions and see what works' is exactly the process that produces an overfit result: trying several versions against the same data and keeping whichever one looks best means the chosen version was partly selected because it happened to fit that data's noise, not because it captured something real — and the researcher has no way to tell, after the fact, how much of the result was genuine signal versus how much was simply the best of several tries. Writing the hypothesis first — the universe, the exact signal definition, the expected direction and magnitude, the success metric, and the kill criteria — before touching the data, commits the researcher in writing to what would count as the idea being wrong, which is the only real defense against quietly rationalizing after the fact why whichever version happened to work 'obviously' made sense all along. I'd frame it practically: the upfront time cost is small compared to the cost of building on, or trusting capital to, a result that turns out to have been fit to noise.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't argue the upfront hypothesis is free — it isn't, and I'd say so directly. What I'd push on is that 'try a few versions and see what works' is the exact mechanism that produces an overfit, noise-fit result, and once you've looked at the data and picked the best-looking version, you've lost the ability to tell whether it's real or lucky. Writing the hypothesis first, including explicit kill criteria, is the only honest defense against rationalizing after the fact — and the time it costs upfront is small next to the cost of later trusting a result that was never really there.
commonMistakes: Pretending writing a hypothesis first costs no time, rather than making the honest cost-benefit case
Not explaining specifically why trying several versions and picking the best produces an overfit result
Missing the point that a written hypothesis guards against after-the-fact rationalization specifically
Framing this as a rule to follow rather than explaining the concrete mechanism it protects against
keyPoints: Writing a hypothesis first has a real, acknowledged upfront time cost
'Try a few versions and see what works' is the exact mechanism that produces an overfit, noise-fit result
A written hypothesis, including kill criteria, is the defense against after-the-fact rationalization
The upfront cost is small compared to the cost of later trusting a result that was fit to noise

Correctly explains why trying several versions produces an overfit result

questions.title: Justifying the Cost of Survivorship-Bias-Free Data
questions.prompt: A budget-conscious manager asks why the team should pay significantly more for a survivorship-bias-free historical database instead of using the cheaper, standard dataset already licensed. How do you make the case?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd frame this as a cost comparison between two different kinds of expense, not 'free versus paid': the cheaper dataset only includes companies or funds that still exist today, silently excluding every one that went bankrupt, was delisted, or shut down after bad performance — which means any backtest run on it systematically overstates historical returns, because it's quietly overweighting survivors and winners. I'd be concrete about the consequence: a strategy's apparent historical edge, measured on survivorship-biased data, could be partly or entirely an artifact of this exclusion rather than a real, tradeable signal, and the cost of discovering that only after allocating real capital to a strategy that doesn't actually work is far larger than the price difference between the two datasets. I'd also point out this isn't a one-time cost tradeoff — every future backtest the team runs inherits the same bias for as long as the cheaper dataset remains the source, compounding the risk across every subsequent research project, not just the current one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reframe the comparison: it's not 'cheap data versus expensive data,' it's 'pay now for accurate data, or pay later when a strategy that looked great on biased data loses real money because its apparent edge was partly just survivorship bias.' The cheaper dataset silently drops every company or fund that failed, which overstates historical returns in a way that's invisible until it's too late, and that bias doesn't just affect today's project — it taints every backtest the team runs on that source going forward. The price difference is small next to the cost of acting on a result that was never really there.
commonMistakes: Framing the decision as 'free versus paid' rather than comparing the real costs of each option
Not explaining concretely how survivorship bias overstates historical returns
Treating this as a one-time cost rather than a compounding risk across every future backtest on the cheaper source
Not connecting the bias to the specific, concrete risk of allocating capital to a strategy that isn't actually real
keyPoints: A non-survivorship-bias-free dataset silently excludes failed/delisted companies or funds
This systematically overstates historical returns by overweighting survivors and winners
The real cost comparison is the data price difference versus the cost of acting on an inflated, false edge
The bias compounds across every future backtest run on the cheaper source, not just the current project

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the mechanism of survivorship bias
Correctly reframes the cost comparison
